```{r setup}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(knitr)

# Render from the project root so these relative paths work
samples <- read_csv("data/processed/samples.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
genus   <- read_csv("data/processed/community_genus_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
family  <- read_csv("data/processed/community_family_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

pby      <- read_csv("outputs/tables/genus_permanova_by_year.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
bdy      <- read_csv("outputs/tables/genus_betadisper_by_year.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
pooled   <- read_csv("outputs/tables/genus_permanova_pooled.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
pcav     <- read_csv("outputs/tables/env_pca_variance.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
gapy     <- read_csv("outputs/tables/genus_gap_models_by_year.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
gapp     <- read_csv("outputs/tables/genus_gap_model_pooled.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
gchg     <- read_csv("outputs/tables/genus_gap_change.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
gsamp    <- read_csv("outputs/tables/genus_gap_samples.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
est      <- read_csv("outputs/tables/colonizer_model_estimates.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
mfit     <- read_csv("outputs/tables/colonizer_model_fit.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sens     <- read_csv("outputs/tables/colonizer_model_sensitivity.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fitted   <- read_csv("outputs/tables/colonizer_model_fitted.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cp_means <- read_csv("outputs/tables/cp_composition_stations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  summarise(m = mean(pct), .by = c(year, impact, cp))
cp1g     <- read_csv("outputs/tables/cp1_genera_at_hi.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

e_       <- function(prefix) est[startsWith(est$parameter, prefix), ]
cpv      <- function(y, g, k) cp_means$m[cp_means$year == y & cp_means$impact == g & cp_means$cp == k]
fp       <- function(g, y) 100 * fitted$p[fitted$impact == g & fitted$year == y]
fmt_p    <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))

# Per-year PERMANOVA rows (square root data)
pyr   <- function(y, mod, trm) pby |> filter(year == y, model == mod, term == trm, transform == "sqrt")
imp10 <- pyr(2010, "impact", "Model")
imp11 <- pyr(2011, "impact", "Model")
env10 <- pyr(2010, "impact + env PCs", "PC1")
env11 <- pyr(2011, "impact + env PCs", "PC1")

# Pooled genus PERMANOVA (all genera): year and impact x year shuffle years within stations
pool_all <- pooled |> filter(genera == "all genera")
pyear <- pool_all |> filter(term == "year_f")
pixn  <- pool_all |> filter(term == "impact:year_f")
pimp  <- pool_all |> filter(term == "Model")
pv    <- function(y, k) 100 * pcav$variance[pcav$year == y & pcav$PC == k]

# Gap models (square root data)
gy        <- function(y, trm) gapy |> filter(year == y, transform == "sqrt", term == trm)
gpool     <- function(trm) gapp |> filter(transform == "sqrt", term == trm)
gpool_raw <- gapp |> filter(transform == "raw", term == "year0")
bg_by_year <- gsamp |> filter(transform == "sqrt") |> summarise(b = mean(background), .by = year)

bHI <- e_("bHI"); dHI <- e_("dHI"); cNI <- e_("c (")
```


## Abstract

After the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill, oil reached deep sea sediment in the Gulf of Mexico, and it is not clear how fast the nematode communities that dominate this sediment return to something resembling unimpacted sites. We used genus level nematode composition and sediment chemistry (aluminum, barium, and hydrocarbons) from nine stations (three heavily impacted, three moderately impacted, three unimpacted) sampled in 2010 and 2011 to ask whether impacted communities moved toward unimpacted ones over a year. Each year was analysed on its own, using Bray-Curtis dissimilarities, PERMANOVA, and a principal component analysis of the environmental variables. Impact level explained `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * imp10$R2)`% of the variation among stations in 2010 (p = `r fmt_p(imp10$"Pr(>F)")`) and `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * imp11$R2)`% in 2011 (p = `r fmt_p(imp11$"Pr(>F)")`), but impact level could not be separated from the environmental gradient with nine stations. Every station, unimpacted ones included, changed between years, and the distance from impacted to unimpacted stations, measured against how much unimpacted stations differ from each other, did not decrease; it grew by about `r sprintf("%.2f", gpool("year0")$estimate)` per year at heavily impacted stations (95% interval `r sprintf("%.2f", gpool("year0")$lower)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", gpool("year0")$upper)`), although the size of that increase depended on the transformation. A clear difference in composition was the share of colonizer nematodes, nearly all of them the genus *Halomonhystera*. A beta binomial model fitted by maximum likelihood put the 2010 odds of a colonizer animal at `r sprintf("%.1f", bHI$odds_ratio)` times higher at heavily impacted stations (95% profile interval `r sprintf("%.1f", bHI$or_lower)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", bHI$or_upper)`). By 2011 the gap had widened, because the share fell at unimpacted stations and stayed near `r sprintf("%.0f", fp("HI", 2011))`% at heavily impacted ones. We found no support for recovery by 2011, although two years of data, three stations per group, and a shift common to all stations limit what we can say.

## Introduction

The Deepwater Horizon blowout in 2010 released oil at about 1,525 m depth for 89 days (Bik et al., 2012), and more than 4.9 million barrels of crude oil and hydrocarbon gases entered the Gulf of Mexico (Baguley et al., 2024). A deep sea plume drifted southwest from the wellhead with the bottom currents and reached the benthic ecosystem (Montagna et al., 2013; Baguley et al., 2024). In that sediment the small animals called meiofauna are abundant and diverse (Rex et al., 2006), and nematodes are the dominant group in the deep sea. They matter beyond their numbers, because their burrowing oxygenates the sediment and moves solutes through it (Sharma et al., 2012).

Nematodes are a sensible place to look for recovery. Meiofauna lack a planktonic larval phase and live in the sediment throughout their life cycle, and they have short generation times and high metabolic rates (Baguley et al., 2024). They spend their whole lives in the sediment, reproduce quickly, and have been reported to recover faster than other meiofauna after disturbance (Brannock et al., 2017). But they are not equally tolerant. Some genera are opportunistic colonizers, while others are persistent and more vulnerable to stressors such as oil, so a community can change in makeup even if total numbers bounce back (Ridall and Ingels, 2021). The colonizer and persister (c-p) scale captures this by scoring each genus from 1 (colonizers, fast reproducing and tolerant of disturbance) to 5 (persisters, slow reproducing and sensitive), and it underlies the widely used maturity index (Bongers, 1990; Bongers and Ferris, 1999). Judging recovery also needs a reference. No two undisturbed sites are identical, so a disturbed site has recovered only when it differs from reference sites by no more than reference sites differ from each other.

Tracking recovery properly takes long records, and ours covers two years. We originally planned to project recovery forward with a state-space simulation, but a model like that cannot be estimated from two time points, so we asked a smaller question and tried to be clear about what a short record can show. We compare community composition across impact levels and then model the share of colonizer nematodes with a likelihood we write ourselves. We ask:

1. Between 2010 and 2011, did nematode communities at impacted stations become more similar to those at unimpacted stations, judged against how much unimpacted stations differ from each other, and how do those differences line up with sediment chemistry (aluminum, barium, and hydrocarbons)?
2. Is the difference between heavily impacted and unimpacted communities carried by colonizer nematodes, and did the colonizer share change differently at heavily impacted stations over the year?

If recovery was under way, we expect the distance from impacted to unimpacted stations to shrink and the colonizer share at heavily impacted stations to fall relative to unimpacted ones. The second question emerged during exploratory analysis, when colonizers stood out as a major source of difference between heavily impacted and unimpacted stations, so that part of the study should be read as exploratory and not confirmatory.

## Methods

### Data and preparation

The data come from nine stations on the deep seafloor: three heavily impacted (HI), three moderately impacted (MI), and three unimpacted (NI), which act as our controls. Each station was sampled in 2010 and 2011, and at each visit the sediment was split into a surface layer (0 to 1 cm) and a deeper layer (1 to 3 cm), which gives `r nrow(samples)` samples. Nematodes were counted and identified to genus where possible, and otherwise to family level. Station-level environmental variables were measured at each visit. We chose four of them: aluminum (Al), barium (Ba), 44 polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH44), and total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPH). Ba, PAH44 and TPH have been used as indicators of oil spill contamination, including at this spill (Montagna et al., 2013), and we include Al as a reference metal that should not track the oil.

We worked at the genus level, since genera carry more ecological information than families and the colonizer question needs them. Two features of the data shaped what follows. The 2010 values are percentages while the 2011 values are counts of roughly 100 animals per sample, so we converted every sample to percent composition. That lets us compare what communities are made of, but not how many animals there are. The genus lists also differ between years (`r n_distinct(genus$genus[genus$year == 2010], na.rm = TRUE)` genera in 2010, `r n_distinct(genus$genus[genus$year == 2011], na.rm = TRUE)` in 2011), partly because of spelling and how finely animals were identified. For that reason each year is analysed on its own, with its own controls, and the one analysis that compares years directly is repeated on only the genera found in both years as a check. The main cleaning steps were small. We treated one genus spelled two ways as a single genus, set aside the six animals (all at one station in 2011) that were identified only to family and rescaled each layer back to 100 percent, treated one blank cell as zero, and recalculated the maturity index because the 2010 values in the workbook looked wrong. The cleaning log with every step is in Supplementary Table S1.

The two layers at a station come from the same spot, so they are not independent pieces of evidence, and counting them as separate would overstate how much data we have. Writing $c_{sik}$ for the count (or, in 2010, the percentage) of genus $k$ in layer $i$ at station-year $s$, we converted each layer to a percentage and then averaged the two,

$$
p_{sik} = 100 \, \frac{c_{sik}}{\sum_k c_{sik}}, \qquad x_{sk} = \frac{p_{s1k} + p_{s2k}}{2}.
$$

That leaves nine station averages per year. Most analyses use $y_{sk} = \sqrt{x_{sk}}$. A few very abundant genera can otherwise dominate any measure of difference and hide what happens among the many rarer ones, and the square root turns them down without ignoring them. As a check we repeated the analyses on $x_{sk}$ itself.

### Comparing whole communities

The equations in this subsection (Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, NMDS stress, and the PERMANOVA statistics) are standard published methods that we applied to our data, not ones we developed. The mixed model and colonizer model equations in the later subsections are specified for this dataset.

To say how different two stations are, we need one number that summarizes dozens of genus percentages. We used the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity (Bray and Curtis, 1957),

$$
\mathrm{BC}_{ij} = \frac{\sum_k |y_{ik} - y_{jk}|}{\sum_k (y_{ik} + y_{jk})},
$$

which is 0 when two stations have exactly the same mix of genera and 1 when they share none. It responds to changes in how common each genus is and ignores genera absent from both samples, which is why it is a standard choice for community data. We calculated it separately for each year.

To see the overall pattern we used non metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS), which draws the stations on a flat map so that stations with similar communities sit close together (Kruskal, 1964). It is a picture and not a test, and it is only approximate because a lot of information is squeezed into two dimensions. The stress statistic reports how much was lost,

$$
\text{Stress} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i<j} (d_{ij} - \hat{d}_{ij})^2}{\sum_{i<j} d_{ij}^2}},
$$

where $d_{ij}$ is the distance between points $i$ and $j$ on the map and $\hat{d}_{ij}$ is the value that best preserves the rank order of the $\mathrm{BC}_{ij}$. As a rough guide, values below about 0.2 are good enough to read the broad layout. The axes have no units, and only the distances between points mean anything.

### Environmental variables

Bray-Curtis is designed for community data, so we did not use it on the environmental variables. They are continuous and measured in different units, and several are strongly skewed. We log transformed Ba, PAH44 and TPH, standardized the four variables (Al, Ba, PAH44, TPH), and ran a principal component analysis (PCA) separately for each year. The first two components (PC1 and PC2) summarize the environmental gradient in a form that can be entered in the PERMANOVA next to impact level. To tie the environment to the community dissimilarities directly, we also ran a principal coordinates analysis (PCoA, which is a PCA applied to the Bray-Curtis matrix) and fitted each environmental variable to its first two axes with `envfit` (Oksanen et al., 2026). That gives each variable an $R^2$ and a permutation p value (9,999 permutations) for how well it lines up with the community differences. We did the PCA within each year because concentrations differ strongly between the two years at the control stations (for example Al and PAH44), so the values may not have been measured the same way and should not be placed on one scale without checking.

### Testing differences among groups

A map can suggest patterns that are not there, especially with nine stations, so we tested the main effects with PERMANOVA (Anderson, 2001). We chose it over an ordinary ANOVA because we are comparing many variables at once and the dissimilarities are not normally distributed, and PERMANOVA makes no such assumption. For a grouping with $a$ groups, $n_g$ members in group $g$, and $N$ stations in total,

$$
SS_T = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i<j} \mathrm{BC}_{ij}^2, \qquad SS_W = \sum_{g=1}^{a} \frac{1}{n_g} \sum_{i<j \in g} \mathrm{BC}_{ij}^2, \qquad SS_A = SS_T - SS_W,
$$

$$
F = \frac{SS_A / (a - 1)}{SS_W / (N - a)}, \qquad R^2 = \frac{SS_A}{SS_T}.
$$

$SS_T$ is the total amount of difference among all the stations, found by squaring and summing every pairwise $\mathrm{BC}_{ij}$. $SS_W$ is the part of that total that sits inside groups, and $SS_A$ is what is left, the difference between groups. $F$ divides the between group part by the within group part, each scaled by its degrees of freedom, so a large $F$ means the groups are more different from each other than members of a group are from each other. $R^2$ is the share of the total difference that the grouping accounts for. The p value comes from shuffling the group labels at random many times, recomputing $F$, and asking what fraction of the shuffles gave an $F$ at least as large as the real one.

For each year we ran two PERMANOVAs on the nine stations (9,999 permutations, whole stations shuffled): impact level alone, and impact level together with PC1 and PC2 of the environmental variables. In the second model we report marginal tests, which assess each term after the others, so that the result does not depend on the order of the terms. Nine stations leave only four residual degrees of freedom once impact and two components are in the model, so the environmental tests are weak and should be read as exploratory. Impact level and the hydrocarbon variables also track each other closely, so the two cannot be cleanly separated. We checked that groups were similarly spread with a test of multivariate dispersion, since PERMANOVA can mistake differences in spread for differences in location.

Separate yearly analyses cannot say whether communities changed between years, so for that we also ran a PERMANOVA on all 18 station-years. Impact level belongs to a station and never changes, while year changes within a station, so the two are not shuffled the same way. For year and the impact by year interaction, which asks whether change over the year differed among impact levels, we shuffled year labels within each station so that each station's pair of observations stayed together (999 permutations). With two years per station there are only 512 distinct arrangements, so the smallest p value we can get is about 0.004. For impact level we averaged each station's two years and shuffled whole stations among groups (9,999 permutations).

### Distance to the controls

Our first question is whether impacted stations got closer to the controls. We measured this directly, separately for each year and using the same Bray-Curtis values as above. For an impacted sample $s$ from layer $\ell$ in year $t$, the distance to control is the mean dissimilarity to the three NI samples from the same year and layer. Controls differ from one another too, so we also need a yardstick for normal variation, which we call the background: the mean dissimilarity over the three pairs of NI samples from that year and layer. The gap is the distance minus the background,

$$
D_{s\ell t} = \frac{1}{3} \sum_{c \in \text{NI}} \mathrm{BC}\big((s,\ell,t),(c,\ell,t)\big), \qquad B_{\ell t} = \frac{1}{3} \sum_{c < c'} \mathrm{BC}\big((c,\ell,t),(c',\ell,t)\big), \qquad G_{s\ell t} = D_{s\ell t} - B_{\ell t}.
$$

A recovered station would have a gap near zero, meaning it sits about as far from the controls as controls sit from each other, and not a distance of zero. We modelled the gap, and not the raw distance, because the background itself changed between years and we did not want that to be mistaken for movement by impacted stations. Within each year we fitted a linear mixed model to the HI and MI samples,

$$
G_{s\ell} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \, MI_s + \beta_2 \, Deep_\ell + u_s + \varepsilon_{s\ell}, \qquad u_s \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2), \quad \varepsilon_{s\ell} \sim N(0, \sigma^2),
$$

where $\beta_0$ is the gap for HI stations in the surface layer, $\beta_1$ is how much smaller or larger the gap is at MI stations, and $\beta_2$ is the difference between the deep and surface layers. The random offset $u_s$ gives each station its own level, since its two layers come from the same spot. Each year therefore has 12 observations from six stations. To compare years we put both years in one model with a year term,

$$
G_{s\ell t} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \, MI_s + \gamma \,(t - 2010) + \delta \, MI_s (t - 2010) + \beta_2 \, Deep_\ell + u_s + \varepsilon_{s\ell t},
$$

where $\gamma$ is the change in gap per year for HI stations, the quantity of interest, and $\delta$ is how much the change differs at MI stations. A negative $\gamma$ means the gap is shrinking, so the community is becoming more similar to the controls. The two years of a station share the same $u_s$. Models were fitted by restricted maximum likelihood with the `nlme` package (Pinheiro and Bates, 2000). With six impacted stations and two years the model is close to a paired comparison, and the intervals are wide.

### A model of the colonizer share

For the second question we wanted a model that we wrote ourselves, so that the size of the effect and its uncertainty come from a likelihood we can inspect. We modelled colonizers, the animals in c-p class 1, because they were the clearest difference between groups. The data are naturally counts: of all animals identified at a station in a year, how many were colonizers? For each station-year we therefore counted the colonizers $y_{st}$ out of all animals $n_{st}$, summed over the two layers. The 2011 counts are in the data. In 2010 we only have percentages, so we reconstructed each sample's size as the number of animals that turns its percentages into whole numbers, falling back on assuming the rarest taxon was a single animal. The reconstructed sizes are mostly between 90 and 130 animals per layer, though a few samples are much smaller. Because this is an approximation, we also refitted the model with all 2010 sizes halved and doubled.

A binomial model would treat every animal as an independent draw with the same chance of being a colonizer. Stations of the same impact level clearly differ from each other by more than that allows, so such a model would claim more certainty than the data support. We let each station's true proportion vary around the group mean $p_{st}$, which gives the beta binomial distribution,

$$
y_{st} \sim \text{BetaBinomial}(n_{st}, p_{st}, \kappa), \qquad
P(y \mid n, p, \kappa) = \binom{n}{y} \frac{B\big(y + p\kappa,\; n - y + (1-p)\kappa\big)}{B\big(p\kappa,\; (1-p)\kappa\big)},
$$

where $B$ is the beta function. The parameter $\kappa$ controls how much stations vary around the group mean. Small values mean a lot of variation, and very large values reduce the model to the ordinary binomial. The mean proportion depends on impact level and year through a logistic regression, which keeps $p_{st}$ between 0 and 1 and lets us read effects as odds ratios,

$$
\text{logit}(p_{st}) = a + b_{HI} \, HI_s + b_{MI} \, MI_s + \big(c + d_{HI} \, HI_s + d_{MI} \, MI_s\big)(t - 2010),
$$

where $HI_s$ and $MI_s$ indicate the impact level of station $s$. Here $a$ is the log odds of colonizers at NI stations in 2010, $b_{HI}$ and $b_{MI}$ are the differences from NI in 2010, and $c$ is the yearly change at NI stations. The terms $d_{HI}$ and $d_{MI}$ are how much the yearly change at HI or MI stations differs from the change at NI stations. $d_{HI}$ is the parameter most relevant to our question. If heavily impacted communities were converging on the controls, their colonizer share would fall relative to the controls and $d_{HI}$ would be negative.

We estimated the seven parameters, collected in $\theta$, by maximum likelihood. That means choosing the values that make the observed counts most probable, or equivalently minimizing the negative log likelihood

$$
-\ell(\theta) = -\sum_{s,t} \log P\big(y_{st} \mid n_{st}, p_{st}(\theta), \kappa\big).
$$

We wrote this function directly and minimized it with `optim` (the BFGS method), starting from the observed proportion at NI stations in 2010. We compared the beta binomial model with a plain binomial model using AIC, which rewards fit but penalizes extra parameters, so a lower value is better.

For uncertainty we used profile likelihood intervals, which we prefer to the usual estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors because they do not assume the likelihood is symmetric, and with 18 observations it often is not. To profile a parameter $\theta_j$, we fix it at a trial value, re-maximize over all the others, and record the result,

$$
\ell_p(\theta_j) = \max_{\theta_{-j}} \ell(\theta_j, \theta_{-j}).
$$

The 95% interval contains every value of $\theta_j$ for which $2\big[\ell(\hat\theta) - \ell_p(\theta_j)\big] \le \chi^2_{1,\,0.95}$, so that the negative log likelihood sits no more than about 1.92 above its minimum. We report estimates on the log odds scale and as odds ratios, $\exp(\theta)$.

The model rests on several assumptions that we cannot fully check. Animals are treated as independent draws given a station's proportion, the reconstructed 2010 sample sizes are treated as known, and seven parameters are estimated from 18 observations. We did not correct for looking at several questions. We carried out all analyses in R (R Core Team, 2026) with the `vegan` (version `r as.character(packageVersion("vegan"))`; Oksanen et al., 2026), `nlme` (version `r as.character(packageVersion("nlme"))`; Pinheiro et al., 2026), `ggplot2` (Wickham, 2016), and tidyverse (Wickham et al., 2019) packages.

## Results

### Communities differ by impact level, most clearly in 2011

```{r}
#| label: fig-nmds
#| fig-cap: "NMDS map of the nine stations in each year (genus level, Bray-Curtis, square root percent). Each year was analysed on its own, so the two panels have separate axes."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/genus_nmds_by_year.png")
```

The genus level maps are drawn separately for each year (@fig-nmds), so positions cannot be compared between the panels. Within each year, stations of the same impact level tend to sit near each other.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-permanova
#| tbl-cap: "PERMANOVA for each year on square root genus data (nine stations, 9,999 permutations). The second model reports marginal tests of impact level and the first two environmental principal components."
#| tbl-colwidths: [10, 36, 20, 12, 12, 10]
pby |>
  filter(transform == "sqrt", !term %in% c("Residual", "Total")) |>
  transmute(
    Year = year,
    Model = ifelse(model == "impact", "Impact alone", "Impact + environment"),
    Term = recode(term, Model = "Impact", impact = "Impact"),
    `R²` = R2, F = F, p = fmt_p(`Pr(>F)`)
  ) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

Impact level accounted for `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * imp10$R2)`% of the variation among stations in 2010 (p = `r fmt_p(imp10$"Pr(>F)")`) and `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * imp11$R2)`% in 2011 (p = `r fmt_p(imp11$"Pr(>F)")`; @tbl-permanova). The 2010 result is borderline and sensitive to the transformation, since the untransformed data gave a smaller p value for 2010 than the square root data did, so we do not want to read much into the difference between the years. The dispersion check raised no concern in either year (p = `r fmt_p(bdy$p[bdy$year == 2010 & bdy$transform == "sqrt"])` and `r fmt_p(bdy$p[bdy$year == 2011 & bdy$transform == "sqrt"])`).

### The environmental gradient is mostly one axis, and it lines up with the community

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca
#| fig-cap: "PCA of the standardized environmental variables (Al, Ba, PAH44, TPH) at the nine stations in each year."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/env_pca_by_year.png")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pcoa
#| fig-cap: "PCoA of the genus level Bray-Curtis dissimilarities in each year, with the environmental variables fitted as arrows. Longer arrows mean a better fit to the community axes."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/genus_pcoa_env.png")
```

PC1 of the environmental PCA explained `r sprintf("%.0f", pv(2010, "PC1"))`% of the variation among stations in 2010 and `r sprintf("%.0f", pv(2011, "PC1"))`% in 2011. In both years Ba, PAH44 and TPH loaded together and Al loaded mainly on PC2, so the hydrocarbon gradient is essentially one axis (@fig-pca). When the variables were fitted to the Bray-Curtis PCoA (@fig-pcoa, @tbl-envfit), Ba, PAH44 and TPH lined up with the community axes in both years, and Al did not.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-envfit
#| tbl-cap: "Environmental variables fitted to the first two PCoA axes of the genus Bray-Curtis dissimilarities (9,999 permutations)."
#| tbl-colwidths: [20, 20, 20, 20]
read_csv("outputs/tables/genus_pcoa_envfit.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(Year = year, Variable = variable, `R²` = r2, p = fmt_p(p)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

Because impact level and the hydrocarbon variables describe much the same difference among stations, the two cannot be cleanly separated in the PERMANOVA. When impact level and PC1 and PC2 were entered together, none of the terms was supported on its own (impact level p = `r fmt_p(pyr(2010, "impact + env PCs", "impact")$"Pr(>F)")` in 2010 and `r fmt_p(pyr(2011, "impact + env PCs", "impact")$"Pr(>F)")` in 2011; PC1 p = `r fmt_p(env10$"Pr(>F)")` and `r fmt_p(env11$"Pr(>F)")`), and only four residual degrees of freedom remained. The separate envfit tests are more informative here because each variable is tested alone. They say that the hydrocarbon variables track the community differences, but not whether the communities respond to the contamination itself or to something else that varies with impact class, such as location.

### Communities changed between years, but not differently by impact level

Combining both years, year accounted for `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * pyear$R2)`% of the variation (p = `r fmt_p(pyear$"Pr(>F)")`), which is close to the smallest p value that 512 within-station arrangements allow. Impact level accounted for `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * pimp$R2)`% (p = `r fmt_p(pimp$"Pr(>F)")`). The impact by year interaction, the term that speaks most directly to convergence, was not detected (R² = `r sprintf("%.2f", pixn$R2)`, p = `r fmt_p(pixn$"Pr(>F)")`). Restricting to the genera found in both years gave the same picture, and the family level analysis from an earlier version of this work did too. Stations at every impact level shifted between 2010 and 2011, so a change in composition by itself is not evidence of recovery.

### Distance to the controls did not decrease

```{r}
#| label: fig-distance
#| out-width: 70%
#| fig-cap: "Gap to the controls for each impacted station in 2010 and 2011 (layers averaged for display). The gap is the mean Bray-Curtis distance to the NI stations minus how far the NI stations are from each other. A value of zero means as close to the controls as the controls are to each other."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/genus_gap_by_year.png")
```

The background dissimilarity among unimpacted stations was `r sprintf("%.2f", bg_by_year$b[bg_by_year$year == 2010])` in 2010 and `r sprintf("%.2f", bg_by_year$b[bg_by_year$year == 2011])` in 2011, so the controls became more alike, which is why the gap and not the raw distance is the quantity to follow. Every impacted station had a larger gap in 2011 than in 2010 (@fig-distance).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mixed
#| tbl-cap: "Gap to the controls (square root genus data). Top: separate mixed models for each year (6 impacted stations, 12 samples). Bottom: one model for both years (24 samples); year is the change in gap per year at HI stations. The surface versus deep layer term is not shown."
#| tbl-colwidths: [28, 16, 18, 22, 16]
bind_rows(
  gapy |> filter(transform == "sqrt", term != "layer1-3 cm") |>
    mutate(Model = paste("Year", year)),
  gapp |> filter(transform == "sqrt", term != "layer1-3 cm") |>
    mutate(Model = "Both years")
) |>
  transmute(
    Model,
    Term = recode(term, "(Intercept)" = "HI gap (intercept)", impactMI = "MI minus HI",
                  year0 = "Change per year (HI)", "impactMI:year0" = "Change per year, MI minus HI"),
    Estimate = estimate,
    `95% CI` = sprintf("(%.3f, %.3f)", lower, upper),
    p = fmt_p(p)
  ) |>
  kable(digits = 3)
```

Within each year, heavily impacted stations sat further from the controls than the controls sit from each other, with a gap of about `r sprintf("%.2f", gy(2010, "(Intercept)")$estimate)` in 2010 and `r sprintf("%.2f", gy(2011, "(Intercept)")$estimate)` in 2011, and moderately impacted stations were closer (@tbl-mixed). Across years, the gap at heavily impacted stations grew by about `r sprintf("%.2f", gpool("year0")$estimate)` per year (95% interval `r sprintf("%.2f", gpool("year0")$lower)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", gpool("year0")$upper)`), and the change at moderately impacted stations did not detectably differ (interval for the difference `r sprintf("%.2f", gpool("impactMI:year0")$lower)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", gpool("impactMI:year0")$upper)`). With untransformed data the estimate was smaller, `r sprintf("%.2f", gpool_raw$estimate)`, and its interval included zero (`r sprintf("%.2f", gpool_raw$lower)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", gpool_raw$upper)`). The direction was the same in both versions and none pointed toward recovery, but the size of the increase depends on the transformation, and with six stations we would not call it precisely estimated.

### Colonizers carry much of the difference

```{r}
#| label: fig-cp
#| fig-cap: "Percent of each community in c-p classes 1 (colonizers) to 5 (persisters) at HI and NI stations. Bars show group means, dots show single stations."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/cp_composition.png")
```

The c-p classes show where the HI and NI communities differ (@fig-cp). Colonizers (c-p 1) made up about `r sprintf("%.0f", cpv(2010, "HI", 1))`% of heavily impacted communities in 2010 and `r sprintf("%.0f", cpv(2011, "HI", 1))`% in 2011, against `r sprintf("%.0f", cpv(2010, "NI", 1))`% and `r sprintf("%.0f", cpv(2011, "NI", 1))`% at unimpacted stations. In both years every heavily impacted station had a larger colonizer share than every unimpacted one. About `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * cp1g$share_of_cp1_at_HI[1])`% of the colonizers at heavily impacted stations belonged to a single genus, *`r cp1g$genus[1]`*, in the family Monhysteridae, so the pattern rests largely on one organism and not on a broad shift across the community.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-colonizer
#| tbl-cap: "Colonizer model estimates (log odds) with 95% profile intervals, and the same values as odds ratios."
#| tbl-colwidths: [32, 16, 21, 31]
est |>
  transmute(
    Parameter = recode(parameter, "a (NI log odds, 2010)" = "a: NI, 2010", "bHI (HI minus NI, 2010)" = "bHI: HI vs NI, 2010", "bMI (MI minus NI, 2010)" = "bMI: MI vs NI, 2010", "c (NI change per year)" = "c: NI, per year", "dHI (HI minus NI, change per year)" = "dHI: HI vs NI, per year", "dMI (MI minus NI, change per year)" = "dMI: MI vs NI, per year"),
    Estimate = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
    `Profile 95% CI` = sprintf("(%.2f, %.2f)", profile_lower, profile_upper),
    `Odds ratio` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)", odds_ratio, or_lower, or_upper)
  ) |>
  kable()
```

The beta binomial model fit far better than a plain binomial (AIC `r sprintf("%.0f", mfit$AIC[mfit$model == "Beta-binomial"])` against `r sprintf("%.0f", mfit$AIC[mfit$model == "Binomial"])`), with $\kappa$ near `r sprintf("%.0f", sens$kappa[sens$scale_2010_n == 1])`, which confirms that stations of the same impact level differ by more than counting error would give. In 2010 the odds of a colonizer animal were about `r sprintf("%.1f", bHI$odds_ratio)` times higher at heavily impacted than at unimpacted stations (95% profile interval `r sprintf("%.1f", bHI$or_lower)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", bHI$or_upper)`; @tbl-colonizer and @fig-profiles). Over the next year the odds at unimpacted stations dropped to about `r sprintf("%.2f", cNI$odds_ratio)` of their earlier value (interval `r sprintf("%.2f", cNI$or_lower)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", cNI$or_upper)`), which in the fitted model is a fall in the colonizer proportion from about `r sprintf("%.0f", fp("NI", 2010))`% to `r sprintf("%.0f", fp("NI", 2011))`% (@fig-fit). At heavily impacted stations the fitted proportion hardly moved (`r sprintf("%.0f", fp("HI", 2010))`% to `r sprintf("%.0f", fp("HI", 2011))`%).

```{r}
#| label: fig-fit
#| fig-cap: "Colonizer proportion at each station (dots) and the beta binomial model's fitted group means (lines)."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/colonizer_fit.png")
```

The difference in yearly change was therefore positive ($d_{HI}$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", dHI$estimate)`, profile interval `r sprintf("%.2f", dHI$profile_lower)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", dHI$profile_upper)`), and its interval excluded zero, so the HI and NI colonizer shares grew further apart. That is the opposite of convergence. The moderately impacted stations fell in between, with intervals that included zero for both the 2010 difference and the yearly change. Halving or doubling the reconstructed 2010 sample sizes barely changed anything ($\hat{d}_{HI}$ stayed between `r sprintf("%.2f", min(sens$dHI))` and `r sprintf("%.2f", max(sens$dHI))`).

```{r}
#| label: fig-profiles
#| fig-cap: "Profile likelihoods for bHI (left) and dHI (right). The 95% interval is the stretch of each curve below the dashed line."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/colonizer_profiles.png")
```

## Discussion

Impacted and unimpacted stations still hosted different communities in 2011, and we found no support for the idea that communities at oil impacted stations had begun to resemble unimpacted ones. The communities differed in both years, and much of that difference came from colonizers, almost all of them *Halomonhystera*. That is what we would expect if opportunistic nematodes are favored where disturbance is strong (Ridall and Ingels, 2021). The colonizer share at heavily impacted stations was about as high in 2011 as in 2010, and the distance from impacted to unimpacted stations did not shrink. We cannot attribute the difference to oil, though. We have no data from before the spill, and impact level is partly tangled with location, since the heavily impacted stations lie close together at one end of the study area, so other things that vary across the area could contribute. We looked at where the stations are but did not test for spatial patterns formally, so we cannot separate location from impact level.

The biggest uncertainty is the shift shared by all stations. Unimpacted stations changed as much as impacted ones, and the positive $d_{HI}$ comes from unimpacted stations losing colonizers while heavily impacted stations did not, not from heavily impacted stations getting worse. The environmental analysis could not settle this either: impact class and the hydrocarbon gradient describe nearly the same difference among stations, and with nine stations per year we cannot say which one the communities follow. Hydrocarbon and metal concentrations also differ strongly between years at the control stations, so the two years may not have been measured on the same scale. The shift shared by all stations could be a real regional change. It could just as well come from differences between the years in how samples were collected, subsampled, or identified. The two years are stored differently, the genus lists differ, and we had to reconstruct the 2010 sample sizes, so two years of data cannot tell these explanations apart. There are also only three stations per group, the distance results depended on the transformation, and the colonizer model estimates seven parameters from 18 observations. Models that separate real change from observation error need longer series than ours (Auger-Méthé et al., 2021; Newman et al., 2023), which is why we dropped the state-space projection we first proposed.

Even though recovery could not be quantified, colonizer dominated communities persisting at the most heavily impacted stations a year after the spill suggest that community composition may remain altered for some time after the initial disturbance. If so, taxonomic and functional measures such as the colonizer share could reveal effects that abundance counts alone would miss.

A record this short can show that impacted and unimpacted communities differ and which animals carry the difference, but not how fast recovery proceeds. The most valuable next step is a longer series. A later survey of the same stations with comparable methods (for example in 2023, if such data exist and can be shared) would let us estimate a recovery rate directly and test how well the first two years predict what came after. Measured hydrocarbon concentrations could also replace the three impact classes as a continuous predictor in the colonizer model.

The data are proprietary and are not in the repository: the original workbook, the cleaned tables, and the tables derived from them stay local, and the scripts rebuild everything from the workbook (see the README for the folder layout).
